questions.question: What is the difference between Server and Client Components in Next.js?
questions.title: Server Vs Client Components
questions.direct_answer: Server Components (the default in App Router) render on the server: they can fetch data directly, access secrets/backends, never ship their code to the browser, and can't use useState/useEffect/event handlers/browser APIs. Client Components ('use client' at the top) are the interactive ones: state, effects, event handlers, browser APIs — at the cost of shipping to the browser. The pattern: keep routes server-rendered and push 'use client' to the LEAVES (buttons, inputs, widgets) — props flow from server components down into client ones.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    SC[Server Component: default] -->|serializable props| CC[Client Component: use client]
    SC --> DB[direct await db / secrets]
    CC --> I[useState, effects, onClick, window]
    CC -->|mutation| SA[Server Action: use server]
    R[RSC payload: tree description, NOT JS] --> HY[hydrate client leaves]
    subgraph rules
        N1[client cannot import server]
        N2[props across boundary must serialize]
    end
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
What actually travels (the mechanism): server components render to a serialized RSC payload (a description of the tree, NOT HTML and NOT JS) — the client runtime materializes client components from it and hydrates them. That's why props crossing the boundary must be serializable (the payload is data) and why server component code never ships: only its OUTPUT description does. On navigation, the same payload stream updates the tree — no full document reload, which is the SPA-like navigation Next.js gives you inside a server-rendered app.

Hydration and its cost model (the perf reality): client components still SSR-render initial HTML (good LCP) then hydrate in the browser (attach event handlers, run effects). Hydration runs the component a second time — a client component tree that is huge means double work and a long 'interactive but not yet' window. This is the technical argument for the leaves-pattern: every component you KEEP server-side is code that never hydrates.

Server Actions (the modern completion): 'use server' functions run ONLY on the server — callable from client components as form actions or transitions. They're the sanctioned 'client triggers server logic' path (mutations without building a REST route), with built-in POST semantics + encryption of closure args. The architecture summary that lands: server components read, server actions write, client components interact — and the boundaries are marked by exactly two directives.
